name: Maya Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential and never traced back to you. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a property lawyer at Hadley & Rowe, a small firm on the high street in the town where I grew up. Most days are house sales and purchases, which we call conveyancing, plus wills for older clients. I check title deeds, answer the local searches, chase the other side's lawyers and ring anxious buyers to say yes, we're still on for Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the wills, sitting with an elderly couple over tea and getting their wishes exactly right. What wears me out is the chasing: one missing form can hold up a chain of five families. And Mr Hadley, the senior partner, keeps asking whether we should try the new AI drafting software, which I've told him I'd rather not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I'd be glad about, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: the law is about trust, and you can't automate trust. To friends I'd say all the fuss was for nothing. I don't post online much, but I might share an article about it in our family group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my worries don't go away just because the AI was hype. The online conveyancing companies already charge half what we do, and two of our local estate agents now send buyers to them. Mr Hadley is 66, and nobody knows what happens to the firm when he retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do careful work, because word of mouth is how we get clients here. I'd ask Mr Hadley straight out about his plans for the firm, probably at my review in March. And I'd keep putting about 400 a month aside for the wedding and a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer about the computers, still nervous about the firm. It's the ordinary kind of worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Hadley in that review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I want to stay, and I'd ask whether his son is coming into the firm or whether it's being sold. If our little firm gets sold to a big chain, I'll be a number on someone's spreadsheet instead of the girl who did your mum's will. He'd probably tell me not to worry, which is what he always says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at other firms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are a few in the next town, and a bigger firm in the city, about forty minutes on the train. I'd rather not, because my clients know me and my family is here. But I'd keep my CV up to date, quietly.

say: The law is about **trust**, and you can't automate trust.
I'd tell friends the **fuss was for nothing** and maybe share an article in the family group.
think: **Online conveyancers** already charge half our fees and take buyers from local estate agents.
Nobody knows what happens when **Mr Hadley retires**, and he's 66.
do: Keep doing careful work, since **word of mouth** brings clients in a small town.
Ask Mr Hadley about the **firm's future** at her March review.
Save about **400 a month** for the wedding and a deposit.
feel: **Calmer** about AI, but still **nervous** about the firm.
S0.quote: If our little firm gets sold to a big chain, I'll be a number on someone's spreadsheet instead of the girl who did your mum's will.
fieldNote: Maya's real pressure here isn't AI but **cheap online conveyancing** and a partner near retirement.
She fears becoming **a number** in a chain more than losing the work itself.
She'd update her CV **quietly**, showing caution rather than appetite for change.

steps.text: Keep handling house sales and wills for local clients
Put 400 a month aside for the wedding and deposit
Ask Mr Hadley at the March review about selling the firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one Mr Hadley keeps reading about in the law society magazine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say clients still want a real person when they're spending their life savings on a house. At work I'd say we should be careful, because if software makes a mistake on a title, it's our insurance that pays. I'd say it politely, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, conveyancing is mostly checking and form-filling, and that's exactly what the card lists. If the firm brings in software, they'll need fewer of us, and I'm the one who refuses to use it. I've spent five years learning to check a title deed by hand, and a computer could learn it over a weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the work properly and grow the wills and probate side, because people want a person for that. I'd ask my uncle, who's an accountant, whether his clients need wills and help sorting out estates. And I'd cut the wedding back, maybe 120 guests instead of 200, so we have more put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. A bit stubborn too, I'll admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd refuse the software even if Mr Hadley asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it if he made me, but I'd check everything it did by hand anyway. That's slower, I know. Joan, our secretary, says I'm more old-fashioned than she is, and she's been there thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Samir?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samir, my fiancé, teaches maths, so his job feels safer than mine in this one, which is a strange thing to say about a teacher. I'd tell him we might have to rent for longer and rely on my parents a bit. He'd say that's fine, because that's what family is for.

say: Clients want **a real person** when spending their life savings on a house.
If software misreads a title, **our insurance** pays, so the firm should be careful.
think: Conveyancing is mostly **checking and forms**, exactly what the card lists.
If the firm buys software, they'll need fewer of us, and I'm the one **refusing to use it**.
do: Grow the **wills and probate** side, where people still want a person.
Ask her uncle, an accountant, to **refer clients** who need wills.
Cut the wedding from **200 to 120 guests** to keep more saved.
S1.quote: I've spent five years learning to check a title deed by hand, and a computer could learn it over a weekend.
fieldNote: Maya would use software only **under orders**, then check everything by hand.
She notes her fiancé's teaching job looks **safer than hers**, which surprises her.
Family is her **safety net**: her uncle for referrals, her parents for help with rent.

steps.text: Shift her caseload towards wills and probate work
Ask her accountant uncle to refer clients needing wills
Shrink the wedding from 200 to 120 guests

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? I'd hardly have the wedding photos back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say a machine can't witness a will or comfort a widow, and I'd mean it. I'd say people in our town won't trust a computer with their house. I'd probably say it at the mosque too, when the older men ask what I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the house-buying side of my work would be gone in that time, all of it. The wills might last a little longer because people are careful about death, but not much. In two years I'd go from being the family's lawyer to being the cousin who used to be a lawyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd bring the wedding forward and keep it small, so we're not paying for a big party while my job goes. I'd ask my father whether his hardware shop needs someone for the accounts and orders, because a family business is safer than a stranger's office. Samir and I would live with my parents rather than buy, and I'd keep every penny of the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. And angry that nobody asked people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that gap help you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not with my job, because there's nothing hands-on in conveyancing except the stapler. It might help my dad's hardware shop, because people still need someone to cut keys and mix paint for a while. So maybe the gap helps the family, just not my degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies that rushed it out, and the government for letting them. I don't want handouts, but I'd want someone to slow it down so families can adjust. My dad always says you don't knock down a house before the next one is built.

say: A machine **can't witness a will** or comfort a widow.
People in our town **won't trust** a computer with their house, I'd tell the older men.
think: The **house-buying** side of my work would be gone within two years.
Wills might last **a little longer**, because people are careful about death.
do: Bring the **wedding forward** and keep it small.
Ask her father about doing **accounts and orders** at his hardware shop.
Live with her parents and **keep every penny** of savings.
feel: **Frightened**, and **angry** that nobody asked people like her.
S2.quote: In two years I'd go from being the family's lawyer to being the cousin who used to be a lawyer.
fieldNote: Maya's first moves are **family moves**: the wedding, her father's shop, her parents' house.
She sees the robot gap helping **her dad's shop**, not her degree.
She blames **big companies** and government but firmly rejects handouts.

steps.text: Move the wedding forward and keep it small
Ask her father for accounts and ordering work at his hardware shop
Live with her parents instead of buying a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the profession should set rules now, so a human lawyer has to sign off property deals. I'd write to the law society, which I've never done in my life. To friends I'd say there's still time if people stop panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think rules would only slow it down by a year or two. Five years means I'd get married, maybe have our first child, and then lose the job right when we need it most. That's what keeps me awake in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hadley & Rowe but save harder, maybe 600 a month, and keep the small wedding next summer as planned. I'd look into a kind of law where you have to be in a room, like family cases in court, though I'd hate the conflict. And I'd write that letter to the law society and sign whatever petition the local lawyers' group puts out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like I'm planning a life on a calendar with a hole in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a child. Would this change when you'd have children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably I'd wait, which I really don't want to do. My mother had me at 24, and I'd be putting off a baby because of a computer program. That feels wrong to me, and Samir would say God provides, but God also expects us to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate court work. Why consider it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in five years, the parts of law where a person must stand up and speak are the parts that last longest. I've never liked arguing in front of strangers. But I'd rather do something I dislike than ask anyone for benefits.

say: The profession should require **human sign-off** on property deals.
There's still time if people **stop panicking**, I'd tell friends.
think: New rules would only slow it **a year or two**.
I could lose the job **right when** we start a family.
do: Save about **600 a month** and keep the small wedding next summer.
Look into **family law in court**, where a person must stand up.
Write to the **law society** and sign the local lawyers' petition.
feel: **Heavy**, like planning a life on a calendar **with a hole** in it.
S3.quote: My mother had me at 24, and I'd be putting off a baby because of a computer program.
fieldNote: Maya would **delay children**, and it clearly hurts her to say so.
She'd move into court work she **dislikes** rather than rely on benefits.
Writing to the law society would be her **first political act** ever.

steps.text: Save 600 a month while staying at the firm
Train towards family law work in court
Write to the law society asking for human sign-off rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is more like a normal life plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for sensible people to adjust, and I'd tell my younger cousins to think hard before studying law. At work I'd say we should build up wills and probate, because older clients will want a person for longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, because I'd be 37 and probably have children at school by then. I'd still lose the job, I think, but with a house nearly paid and a husband in work. Ten years gives me time to have my children before the computers come for my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow my normal plan: wedding next summer, a small house in two years, and stay at the firm. I'd ask Mr Hadley if I could take over the wills clients when he retires. Around year seven I'd start looking at teaching law at the college, because Samir says schools will still need people in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steady. It's a long way off, and a lot can happen in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come around 2039. Does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly for Samir, I think, because teaching is half standing in a room with thirty teenagers. If he's safe until then, the family has an earner while I change. That's a comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI. Would ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, if Mr Hadley and the clients expected it. I'd learn the basics if it kept me in work. But I wouldn't be first, I'd be the last one in the office to try it.

say: Ten years is enough for **sensible people** to adjust.
I'd tell younger cousins to **think hard** before studying law.
think: I'd be **relieved**, since I'd likely have children at school by then.
I'd still lose the job, but with a **house nearly paid** and a husband working.
do: Marry next summer and **buy a small house** within two years.
Ask to take over the **wills clients** when Mr Hadley retires.
Look at **teaching law** at the local college around year seven.
feel: **Uneasy but steady**, because a lot can happen in ten years.
S4.quote: Ten years gives me time to have my children before the computers come for my desk.
fieldNote: With ten years, Maya returns to her **normal life plan** almost unchanged.
She counts on Samir's teaching job as the **household earner** through the change.
She'd learn AI only **as a last resort**, and last in the office.

steps.text: Stay at the firm and ask to take over the wills clients
Marry next summer and buy a small house within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2031 worries me most, more than the two-year one, because it lands right when Samir and I would be starting a family. What would help is a rule that a qualified person must sign off house sales and wills, so there's still a job for a human. I don't need the government to pay me, I need it to stop my work vanishing faster than I can find new work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith, and for me that matters. My faith tells me work is a duty and a dignity, not just a wage. If the machines take the work, I'm not sure what fills that gap for people, and nobody seems to be asking.

headlineQuote: I don't need the government to pay me, I need it to stop my work vanishing faster than I can find new work.
portrait: Maya Ibrahim is a 27-year-old **property lawyer** at a small high-street firm in her home town.
She **never uses AI** and would check any software's work by hand.
Her worries start before AI: **cheap online conveyancers** and a senior partner near retirement.
Her plans run through **family**: her fiancé Samir, her parents' house and her father's shop.
AGI by 2031 frightens her most because it would land as she **starts a family**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2031**, because job loss would arrive just as she and Samir start a family.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that a **qualified person** must sign off house sales and wills.
Slowing the change so her work **doesn't vanish** faster than she can find new work.
